challenges.title: Valid Palindrome
challenges.prompt:
A phrase counts as a palindrome if, after turning uppercase letters into lowercase and dropping every character that is not a letter or a digit, it reads the same forward and backward.

Given a string `s` of printable ASCII characters, return `true` if it is a palindrome under this rule and `false` otherwise. Try to use O(1) extra space.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

examples.explain: Cleaned, it is "raceacar", which reversed is "racaecar".

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?

hints: Put one pointer at each end and move them toward each other.
Before comparing, move each pointer past characters that are not letters or digits, without letting the pointers cross.
Compare lowercase versions. Digits count: "0P" is not a palindrome.
challenges.explanation: Converging pointers compare characters from both ends, skipping anything that is not a letter or digit. Each skip loop is guarded by lo < hi so a string with no letters cannot push a pointer out of range. No cleaned copy is built, so extra space is O(1).

challenges.title: Two Sum on a Sorted Array
challenges.prompt:
Given an array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order and an integer `target`, return the indexes `[i, j]` with `i < j` of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

Exactly one answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice. Use only O(1) extra space.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Start with one pointer at each end of the array.
If the sum is too small, which pointer can make it bigger? If it is too big, which one can make it smaller?
Each move discards an element that cannot be in any remaining pair. Stop when the pointers meet.
challenges.explanation: Sorted order makes moves predictable: a sum that is too small means nums[lo] is too small for every remaining partner, so lo moves right; a sum that is too big eliminates nums[hi]. Each step discards one element, so the scan is linear and needs no extra memory.

challenges.title: 3Sum
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums`, return every unique triple of values `[a, b, c]` taken from three different positions such that `a + b + c == 0`.

The answer must not contain the same triple twice. Triples, and the values inside each triple, may be in any order.

examples.explain: The two -1s are different positions, so [-1, -1, 2] is allowed.
Many position choices give the same triple; report it once.

hints: Sort the array. Then, for each first value nums[i], you need a pair in the rest that sums to -nums[i].
Find that pair with converging pointers on nums[i + 1:].
Skip a first value equal to nums[i - 1], and after recording a triple, move lo past values equal to the one just used.
challenges.explanation: Sorting lets each first value turn the rest into a pair-sum sweep. Duplicates are skipped in two places: equal first values (compare with the previous one, so the first copy is still used) and equal lo values after a match. The early break works because a positive first value means every later value is positive too. In JavaScript, remember the numeric comparator, since the default sort compares as strings.

complexity.space: O(1) extra besides the output and the sort

challenges.title: Container With Most Water
challenges.prompt:
You are given an array `height` where `height[i]` is the height of a vertical line drawn at position `i`. Any two lines, together with the x-axis, form a container. The water it holds is the shorter line's height times the distance between the lines.

Return the largest amount of water any container can hold. Aim for O(n).
hints: Start with the widest container: one pointer at each end.
The shorter line caps the water level. Can any narrower container that keeps the shorter line do better?
Record the area, then move the pointer at the shorter line inward. Repeat until the pointers meet.
challenges.explanation: Start wide and shrink. Every remaining container is narrower, and any that keeps the shorter line is capped at its height, so the shorter line cannot be in a better container and can be discarded. With equal heights, either side may move. One pass, constant space.

challenges.title: Remove Duplicates From a Sorted Array
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates in place so that each value appears once, keeping the original order, and return the number of unique values `k`.

After your function runs, the first `k` slots of `nums` must hold the unique values. What is left in the slots after them does not matter. Use O(1) extra space: no second array. The tests check the returned `k`, but write it the way an interviewer expects, with `nums` updated in place.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Duplicates in a sorted array sit next to each other.
Keep a write index for where the next unique value goes, and scan with a read index.
A value is new when it differs from the last value you kept, nums[write - 1]. Handle the empty array first.
challenges.explanation: The invariant is that nums[:write] holds the unique values seen so far. Because the array is sorted, a value is new exactly when it differs from the last kept value; copy it to nums[write] and advance. write ends as the count of unique values.

challenges.title: Trapping Rain Water
challenges.prompt:
Each value in `heights` is the height of a bar of width 1, and the bars stand side by side. After heavy rain, water collects in the dips between bars. Return the total units of water held.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

examples.explain: Water rises to height 3 between the walls 3 and 4: 3 + 1 + 3 units above the three inner bars.

hints: The water above bar i rises to the lower of the tallest bar on its left and the tallest bar on its right (counting bar i itself), so it holds `min(maxLeft, maxRight) - heights[i]`.
Two arrays of running maximums give O(n) time and O(n) space. To drop the arrays, move two pointers inward from both ends and track `leftMax` and `rightMax`.
Move the side with the lower bar. If `heights[left] < heights[right]`, the right side already has a wall at least that tall, so the water at `left` is decided by `leftMax` alone.

solution.python:
def trap_water(heights):
    left, right = 0, len(heights) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while left < right:
        if heights[left] < heights[right]:
            # A wall at least this tall waits on the right, so left_max decides the level here.
            left_max = max(left_max, heights[left])
            water += left_max - heights[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, heights[right])
            water += right_max - heights[right]
            right -= 1
    return water

challenges.explanation: The level above a bar is min(tallest on the left, tallest on the right). With two pointers you only need the smaller of those two: when heights[left] < heights[right], some bar on the right is at least as tall as anything seen on the left, so the level at left is exactly leftMax. Each step settles one bar, so the scan is O(n) with four variables. A monotonic stack that fills water layer by layer is another O(n) answer.
